title: The Mill on the Floss: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Mill and Its Shadows

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we're going to spend serious time with one of the great novels in the English language.

A novel about a family on the edge of ruin, a girl of fierce intelligence in a world that has no place for her, and the question of whether loyalty and love can survive the weight of everything life brings down on us.
George Eliot published The Mill on the Floss in 1860, and it has never stopped being read, argued over, and felt.
Today we open with the mill itself — its shadows, its rhythms, and what this novel asks of us from the very first pages.
And I have three extraordinary readers with me to do it justice.

Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive — he hears the prose as performance, catches the comic timing and the emotional weight that's written into the rhythm of the sentences themselves.
He brings the novel off the page and into the room.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who specialises in the institutions that fiction depicts — the law, the money, the social machinery.
He will tell us what was actually at stake when the Tullivers lost the mill — and why Eliot's social diagnosis is still startlingly current.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.
She reads for the experience — the sentences that stop you, the characters who deserve better, the passages you need to read aloud to someone else immediately.
Let's begin.
What strikes me every time I come back to this novel — and I have come back to it many times in the recording booth — is how immediately it puts you inside a consciousness.
Eliot is not just telling you a story. She is thinking at you.
And there is a particular passage — a moral aside from the narrator — that I think announces the whole novel's project.

"It is easy enough to spoil the lives of our neighbours without taking so much trouble; we can do it by lazy acquiescence and lazy omission, by trivial falsities for which we hardly know a reason, by small frauds neutralised by small extravagances, by maladroit flatteries, and clumsily improvised insinuations."
That is not the villain's speech. That is the novel's whole moral universe in four lines.
Nobody in this book is deliberately wicked. Everyone is just a little bit lazy, a little bit careless, a little bit self-serving.
And the damage accumulates. Quietly. Inexorably.
Oliver has put his finger on something that I think is genuinely radical about this novel.
Eliot writes — and this is the passage Oliver just read — that plotting covetousness and deliberate contrivance are "nowhere abundant but in the world of the dramatist."
She is directly arguing against the melodramatic tradition — against the idea that harm requires a villain with a plan.

When I look at the actual history of how families like the Tullivers were destroyed — by debt, by legal process, by the quiet turning of community against them — it maps onto this passage with uncomfortable precision.
Nobody forecloses on a neighbour with mustache-twirling malice. They just call in what is legally owed.
"We live from hand to mouth, most of us, with a small family of immediate desires." That line is both a social observation and a precise legal description of the Tulliver household.
What I find remarkable is that Eliot writes that passage in the first person plural. Not "they" — "we."
"We can do it by lazy acquiescence." She is including herself. She is including the reader.
That is an extraordinarily uncomfortable thing to do in a novel about a family being slowly ground down by their community.
You cannot read this as a portrait of bad people somewhere else. It becomes a mirror.
And that is the experience of reading this novel — you keep catching your own reflection in it.
That is what makes it so difficult to put down, and so difficult to dismiss.
There is another passage I keep returning to that shows how Eliot builds the human cost of all this into the tiniest domestic detail.
It concerns Tom, alone at school after Maggie has been fetched home.
"When this small apparatus of shallow quickness was fetched away in the gig by Luke, and the study was once more quite lonely for Tom, he missed her grievously."
"Small apparatus of shallow quickness" — that is one of Eliot's devastating comic phrases, and it is also a kind of tenderness.
She is gently mocking Maggie's mercurial cleverness at the same moment she is showing us how much Tom depended on it.

And then we learn he had "actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar."
"A dim understanding." That is a writer who is funny and heartbroken at exactly the same time.
That passage undoes me a little, every time.
Because Maggie has been asking the questions — about the Roman Empire, about whether anyone actually said those Latin phrases — and Tom is the one who quietly benefits.
He gets a richer historical imagination because of her. And she is sent home.
The inequality is never stated. It is just there, in the structure of the sentences.
That is what I mean when I say this novel earns every re-read. You see different things each time, at different points in your own life.
What Caroline is describing is the structural injustice that the novel never has to argue for explicitly, because it simply depicts it.
Tom is at school because the family is stretching every resource to give him a professional education — an investment that will prove catastrophically ill-judged, given his actual aptitudes.
Maggie stays home because girls stayed home. That was not a choice — it was a social fact as fixed as the mill itself.
And Eliot makes us feel both the waste and the specific texture of daily life inside that constraint — which is considerably harder to do than simply arguing against it.
And that tension — between the life that is lived and the life that might have been — runs like a current through everything that follows.
Later in the novel, Mr Tulliver says something to Maggie that is only seven words long and yet stops the reader completely.
"Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er."
Seven words. A whole life's loss in them.
And then Maggie, near the end of the novel, articulates the cost of faithfulness in a way that matches that loss — and exceeds it in anguish.
"Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves. They mean renouncing whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us."
Those two lines — the father's and the daughter's — frame the whole emotional architecture of this book.
In our next segment, we turn to the Dodson sisters — the aunts, the family code, and the social world that made the Tullivers who they are.

segments.title: The Merchant and His Debts: Mr Tulliver's Fall

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're going deep into one of the novel's great engines of tragedy: Mr Tulliver's ruin.
Not just the financial collapse, but the pride, the obstinacy, the almost operatic self-defeat that drives it.
With me as always is Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the man who has read more classic novels aloud than any living person.
Oliver hears the rhythms of Eliot's prose in a way that consistently surprises me.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what it meant, in practical terms, to fall into debt in provincial England.
James will keep us honest about the world outside the novel's pages.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since her teens and reads it with the kind of attention that changes what you notice.
Let's begin with Mr Tulliver's extraordinary letter to Mrs Glegg.
That letter is one of the great comic detonations in the novel.
Eliot sets it up perfectly — Mrs Glegg is sitting in full glow of her own magnanimity, expecting gratitude.
And instead she receives this.
"she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children."
He pays her back, and he insults her, in the same breath.
The timing of that letter — arriving the very evening of Mrs Pullet's departure — is exquisite.
Tulliver has wounded her at the precise moment she was most armoured against humility.
What strikes me is how completely Eliot understands both of them in this moment.
Mrs Glegg's satisfaction in her own loftiness is so precisely described — she genuinely believes herself to be magnanimous.
And Tulliver's letter is not cruelty — it's dignity, as he understands dignity.
He can't accept her money and also accept her condescension.
The tragedy, of course, is that the money he's using to repay her is money he shouldn't be spending.
His pride is already mortgaging his children's future.
That repayment matters enormously in legal and social terms.
Family loans in this period occupied a peculiar position — they were private debts but they carried public honour obligations.
Mrs Glegg's five hundred pounds is not merely money — it's leverage, and Tulliver knows it.
By repaying her, he severs that leverage — he frees himself from one creditor, but he destabilises himself financially to do it.
It's a decision that makes perfect psychological sense and near-perfect financial nonsense.
And Eliot is completely alive to that paradox — she doesn't judge him, but she doesn't spare him either.
There's a passage about Mrs Tulliver's influence on her husband that I find almost unbearably funny.
"it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back"
The 'credit or discredit' — she cannot resist distributing moral blame even in the act of distributing metaphor.
That is a writer at full stretch.
But Eliot immediately complicates it — she says the blame ought to lie with the previous weight of feathers, not with Mrs Tulliver's single contribution.
It's a defence of Mrs Tulliver, quietly inserted into what sounds like satire.
And the key detail is that Tulliver doesn't really hear his wife at all — he hears the Dodsons through her.
She becomes a symbol of the family whose dominance he cannot bear to acknowledge.
She is invisible to him as a person, even as she stands in his path.
That invisibility has a legal dimension too.
A married woman in this period had no independent legal standing — coverture meant she was subsumed into her husband's legal identity.
So Tulliver's erasure of Mrs Tulliver as an individual is not merely personal psychology — it mirrors the law.
Eliot is doing something rather pointed here, I think.
And hovering over all of this, of course, is Wakem.
The attorney who becomes the focus of Tulliver's rage — almost a gothic villain in his imagination.
Wakem is one of Eliot's great grotesques — seen entirely through Tulliver's furious, distorting lens.
Eliot gives us Tulliver's verdict on him in a sentence of pure comic venom.
"A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!"
The exclamation marks are doing real work there — you can hear Tulliver's voice, practically spitting.
And then the wonderful aside — he's irritated that his own lawyer Gore isn't more like Wakem.
He has just enough self-awareness to know he's backing the weaker horse.
The paranoia about Wakem is historically recognisable.
Country attorneys in the first half of the nineteenth century were genuinely powerful figures — they could shape outcomes, broker deals, orchestrate litigation.
A miller with no legal sophistication, facing a lawyer who acts on multiple sides of disputes, was genuinely vulnerable.
Tulliver's conviction that Wakem is 'at the bottom of' all his troubles may be paranoid in degree, but not entirely without foundation.
Eliot knew enough about the law to make the satire bite.
What moves me is the note of bitter comedy in the detail about Tulliver having to take his own business to Wakem's office.
He hates this man with everything in him — and circumstance has forced him to be this man's client.
That is the specific texture of humiliation that Eliot is so good at rendering.
It accumulates — and we feel, even through the comedy, how much has already been lost before the ruin formally arrives.
The ruin doesn't stay with the adults, of course — it falls hardest on the children.
James, you wanted to talk about what Maggie carries through all of this.
There's a passage about Maggie after the ruin that I find almost unbearable in its precision.
Eliot writes about what it is to be young and deprived of love — not sentimental about it at all.
"There is no hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants, and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others."
That phrase — 'no superadded life in the life of others' — is describing what poverty does to the imagination.
Adults survive despair partly by borrowing from the lives and histories they've accumulated.
Maggie has nothing to borrow from.
And Eliot immediately catches herself — and us.
'though we who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the future lightened the blind sufferer's present.'
She's addressing us directly — the comfortable readers — and she's accusing us.
We know Maggie's story has a future; Maggie doesn't.
Our knowledge doesn't help her — it only lets us dismiss her pain more easily.
And it links forward to Tom — because Tom has appointed himself the keeper of the family's respectability through all of this.
There's the scene where he confronts Maggie about Philip Wakem — and forces her to swear on the Bible.
"I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you."
The righteousness is real — that's what makes it so cold.
Tom is not performing virtue — he has genuinely sacrificed himself, and he genuinely cannot understand why Maggie won't do the same.
Tom's speech has an internal logic that is almost airtight, and that is exactly what makes it devastating.
He says: 'what is the use of my exerting myself and giving up everything else for the sake of paying my father's debts, if you are to bring madness and vexation on him'?
He has subordinated his entire life to a social and financial project — clearing the debt, restoring the name.
And from within that project, Maggie's inner life simply does not compute.
Tom is his father's son in the most painful way.
Tulliver couldn't hear Mrs Tulliver because he saw only the Dodsons through her.
Tom can't hear Maggie because he sees only the threat to duty and respectability through her.
The people they love most become abstractions to both men.
That is a devastating thread to pull through the whole segment.
Mr Tulliver's ruin is not simply a financial catastrophe — it's a pattern of erasure that the next generation inherits.
In our next segment, we'll turn to what survives the ruin — what Maggie reaches for when the world contracts around her.
Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've spent time with the novel's world — its rivers, its mills, its creditors and aunts.
Now we turn to the mind at the novel's centre: Maggie Tulliver.
The child Maggie — jealous, impulsive, capable of breathtaking imaginative leaps — is one of the great characters in English fiction.
And the way George Eliot renders her interior life, even in these early chapters, is extraordinary.
To explore that, I'm joined again by Oliver Trevelyan, our performer and close listener of prose.
By Professor James Blackstone, whose eye for social context keeps us honest about what the novel's world actually cost.
And by Caroline Woodcourt, who has been reading and re-reading this novel since she was a teenager and knows it more intimately than almost anyone.
Oliver, let's start with you — because you've said the child chapters are where Eliot earns everything that comes later.
She absolutely earns it, and she earns it through something quite ruthless — she lets Maggie be genuinely unpleasant.
Not poetically tragic. Not misunderstood. Actually, in this moment, thinking cruel thoughts about a small child who has done nothing wrong.
There's a passage I want to read, because the writing is so precise it almost hurts.
"Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse."
A little white mouse. That's the comparison Eliot reaches for. Not a sparrow or a kitten — a mouse.
Something small, defenceless, slightly pathetic — and Lucy is all of those things to Maggie in this moment.
And then comes the action she's actually contemplating: slapping or pinching Lucy — specifically to vex Tom.
The logic is perfect child logic. Tom doesn't feel slaps, so the cruelty must be redirected to someone he cares about.
What strikes me every time I read that passage is the word 'actually.'
'She was actually beginning to think' — that 'actually' is doing so much quiet work.
It's the narrator registering surprise — or performing surprise — at the depths Maggie is capable of reaching.
And what's devastating is that it isn't just jealousy over Tom's affection.
It's that Maggie had been the one doing the loving before — petting Lucy, making much of her — and Tom has simply stepped in and taken over without effort.
The injustice of that, to a child like Maggie, is total.
There's something worth pausing on in the social geometry of this scene.
Lucy is the pretty, compliant girl — already fitted for the world she will inherit.
Maggie is the difficult one. Too clever, too dark, too loud.
And Tom — who has done nothing to earn it — simply turns his attention, and the whole equilibrium shifts.
This is precisely the structure Maggie will live inside for the rest of the novel: other people arranging the world around values she cannot satisfy.
And the escape she invents is magnificent — because it is simultaneously completely absurd and completely earned.
She's going to run away to the gypsies.
Eliot sets it up with tremendous deadpan control — listen to this:
"The resolution that gathered in her mind, after Tom and Lucy had walked away, was not so simple as that of going home."
'Not so simple as that of going home.' The understatement is doing all the work.
And then the logic of why the gypsies specifically — she had been told she was like a gypsy, and half wild.
So she is going to inhabit the insult. Turn opprobrium into a destination.
And the planning. The beautifully, painfully specific planning.
She thinks of her father, and she reconciles herself to parting from him — by determining to send a letter via a small gypsy.
A small gypsy who will run away without telling where she is.
The tenderness she has for her father, even in the middle of her most dramatic fantasy — it's heartbreaking.
And entirely consistent: Maggie's imagination doesn't eliminate love, it just accommodates it within the escape plan.
It's worth noting what the gypsy fantasy actually represents — which is not wildness, precisely, but status.
She expects the gypsies to receive her with respect, on account of, as Eliot puts it, her superior knowledge.
Maggie wants to go somewhere her intelligence will be valued rather than treated as a nuisance or a defect.
The tragedy is that she is nine years old and already knows such a place does not exist in her actual world.
Of course, the fantasy does not survive contact with actual gypsies.
And this is where Eliot becomes something very close to a comic novelist of genius — while being simultaneously entirely serious.
The ideas about the gypsies, Eliot tells us, undergo a rapid modification.

"From having considered them very respectful companions, amenable to instruction, she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking."
'Gradual cooking.' Two words. I have never recovered from those two words.
The specificity of the child's fear — not just killed, but cooked gradually, as if the preparation matters.
And then the Devil. Because of course an old man with fierce eyes must be the Devil in disguise.
What I love is that Eliot doesn't mock this. She enters it absolutely.
There's that remarkable detail about Maggie wondering whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts.
"She wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded, whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts."
No theologian could have exceeded that keenness of interest. She is terrified and intellectually engaged simultaneously.
That is Maggie Tulliver in a single sentence.
That passage does something quite precise philosophically, even if it arrives as comedy.
Maggie is caught between two fears: the fear of what the gypsies might do, and the fear of offending them by letting them see her fear.
She is managing a social performance under conditions of existential terror.
That is not a child's problem. That is Maggie's problem for the whole novel.
You can trace that straight through to the adult Maggie — and to what Tom can never understand about her.
Eliot's analysis of Tom's mind is one of the most devastating passages in the novel — and it arrives with the controlled precision of a legal brief.
Here it is, and I want to read it slowly because it rewards that:
"Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye — however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation."
'It is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas.' That void. That is the key.
Tom has no inner life in the sense Maggie has one — so inherited certainty fills the space where thought might otherwise live.
What makes it devastating rather than merely cruel is that Eliot also acknowledges what Tom does have.
Strength of will, conscious rectitude, great self-control. These are not nothing.
In the world the novel depicts, those qualities get results. Tom clears the family debt. He is effective.
But Eliot is relentless about what they cost. They cost Maggie everything.
And there's the end of that passage — 'but of course Maggie could do as she liked, she had declared her determination to be independent.'
"But of course Maggie could do as she liked — she had declared her determination to be independent."
The cold contempt in that 'of course.' Tom isn't even angry at this point — he's simply withdrawn.
It's a prejudice, as Eliot says, that functions as a staff and a baton simultaneously.
Support for himself, a weapon against others. The dual function of inherited conviction.
And the Wakem hatred is the perfect vessel for it — it arrives from the father already formed, already righteous, needing no examination.
What Eliot is describing is not unique to Tom Tulliver. It is a structural feature of a certain kind of character, in any era.
James, that word — 'bequeathed' — connects, doesn't it, to the other great bequest in the novel: Mr Tulliver's own broken sense of the world.
There's a moment near the end of Tulliver's life where he says something that has stayed with me since I first read this novel.
"We shall never be young again — this world's been too many for me."
'Too many for me.' It's only five words, but it carries the weight of the whole novel's first half.
We'll pick up that thread — the fathers, the failures, the debts that can never quite be repaid — in our next segment.

segments.title: Wit, Shame, and the Social Order

utterances.text: Welcome to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked, a close reading of George Eliot's great novel of provincial life, passion, and the price of being born the wrong kind of person in the wrong kind of place.
Today's segment is called Wit, Shame, and the Social Order — and it concerns the comedy Eliot builds around respectability, ambition, and the peculiar tyranny of family tradition.
I'm joined by three guests who bring very different eyes to this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan has lent his voice to more classic novels than anyone alive, and he reads George Eliot the way George Eliot deserves — as performance, as timing, as pleasure.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who knows exactly what these institutions looked like from the inside — and what they cost the people living inside them.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has been reading this novel since her teens and brings to it the love of someone who knows every sentence and still finds new things in them.
Oliver, let's begin with the Dodsons — because Eliot's portrait of that family is one of the great comic set-pieces in English fiction.
The Dodsons are one of those comic creations you feel Eliot genuinely enjoyed writing — you can almost hear her chuckling as she sets up the machinery.
What makes them irresistible is that they are completely, serenely, imperturbably convinced of their own rightness.
There's a passage that captures it absolutely — and you have to hear it read aloud to get the full effect.
"A female Dodson, when in 'strange houses,' always ate dry bread with her tea, and declined any sort of preserves, having no confidence in the butter."
No confidence in the butter.
That's the whole joke — and the whole worldview — in four words.
The Dodsons don't distrust other people's butter because they've been wronged by it — they distrust it on principle, because it is not Dodson butter.
And Eliot makes clear that Mrs Tulliver is a thorough Dodson — she just happens to be the mild version, what the narrator calls 'very weak ale.'
What I love about that passage is the formal symmetry of the satire — Eliot gives with one hand and takes with the other.
She tells us the Dodsons conducted funerals with peculiar propriety — hats, gloves, scarfs for the bearers, all correct.
And then she adds, quietly, that when one of the family was in trouble, the others would visit and 'did not shrink from uttering the most disagreeable truths that correct family feeling dictated.'
'Correct family feeling' — it's magnificent.
The cruelty is institutionalised as virtue, and everyone is perfectly comfortable with the arrangement.
There's something very recognisable about it, isn't there — that particular blend of genuine solidarity and merciless judgment that some families run on.
The Dodsons are funny, yes — but they're also doing something real and historically specific, which is constructing a form of social capital out of nothing but reputation.
For families of that class — minor provincial gentry, tradespeople with pretensions — respectability was quite literally an asset that could be cashed in.
Marriage prospects, creditworthiness, standing in disputes — all of it depended on whether people thought well of you.
So the obsession with bleaching linen correctly and keeping the bottled gooseberries just so — that's not mere fussiness.
It is the visible performance of a creditworthy character, conducted every day, before an audience that is always watching.
James has put his finger on something — and it makes the comedy darker, doesn't it.
There's a passage about Mr Tulliver that works the same way — Eliot catches him in a moment of fine self-deception.
He's decided, impulsively, to repay Mrs Glegg her five hundred pounds — a bold gesture — and he immediately starts working out how it needn't look inconvenient.
Eliot's narrator observes, in that magnificent deadpan way of hers, that
"for getting a strong impression that a skein is tangled there is nothing like snatching hastily at a single thread."
That's a perfect diagnosis of a certain kind of decisive man — the more tangled the situation, the more he needs to act quickly and call it clarity.
Mr Tulliver is genuinely likeable — but Eliot never lets him off the hook.
It's what makes Eliot so extraordinary as a satirist — she can be merciless and fond at the same time.
And she turns that same double vision on Maggie — the comedy about Maggie's education is as clear-eyed as anything she does with the adults.
There's a line that stops me every time I read it — about the peculiar shape of Maggie's mind.
"In travelling over her small mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected knowledge."
'Her small mind' — it sounds almost condescending, and then you realise Eliot means it with complete tenderness.
Maggie has deduced that 'poly' means 'many' from reading the dictionary — but she had no idea gypsies were not well supplied with groceries.
A child like that is both wonderful and heartbreaking in equal measure.
And that gap between what Maggie feels and what she can actually do — Eliot uses it for one of the great comic-tragic moments in the whole novel.
Maggie pushing little Lucy into the mud.
The narrator frames it in this extraordinary way — let me read it, because you really need the full sentence.

"There were passions at war in Maggie at that moment to have made a tragedy, if tragedies were made by passion only; but the essential τι μέγεθος which was present in the passion was wanting to the action."
And then the deflation — 'the utmost Maggie could do, with a fierce thrust of her small brown arm, was to push poor little pink-and-white Lucy into the cow-trodden mud.'
'Pink-and-white Lucy.' 'Cow-trodden mud.'
The Greek philosophical term and the cow-trodden mud — that is Eliot's range in a single sentence.
There's a structural irony there that goes beyond the comedy, though.
Maggie has the inner life for a tragedy — the passion, the moral complexity — but she lacks the social scale that tragedy traditionally requires.
She is a miller's daughter in a provincial town — the institution of her life will not stage her grief properly.
And Eliot knows this — which is why that invocation of the Greek term lands so hard.
It's a formal signal: Maggie belongs in a different kind of story.
Eliot turns that same satirical instrument on the world Maggie must navigate — the clergymen, the schoolmasters, the institutional men.
Mr Stelling is a masterpiece of comic ambition — a man whose certainty about his own future greatness is so total that the facts simply cannot reach him.
Eliot gives us his logic in one of those beautiful sentences where the satire is disguised as plain description.

"A clergyman who has such vigorous intentions naturally gets a little into debt at starting; it is not to be expected that he will live in the meagre style of a man who means to be a poor curate all his life."
'Naturally.' That word is doing all the work.
The debt is presented as self-evidently reasonable — because success is certain, the expenditure simply precedes the income by a modest interval.
It is the logic of every man who has ever ruined himself in complete confidence.
And he's the man who will teach Tom — which tells you something immediately about Tom's education and its limits.
Stelling is brilliant on the surface and empty at the centre — broad-chested, sonorous-voiced, doctrinally flexible, always ready to preach in whatever style is 'the telling thing' in the diocese.
He plans eventually to edit a Greek play and 'invent several new readings' — he has told his wife this, and she has complete confidence in him.
He has not yet selected the play.
That tiny detail — that is Eliot's genius for timing.
Stelling embodies something Eliot returns to throughout the novel — the professional man who has confused the performance of merit with merit itself.
He preaches in an impressive manner — he has memorised Massillon and Bourdaloue — and his hearers find his own feebler passages equally striking because they are delivered in the same loud tone.
The audience cannot tell the difference — and so, in a real social sense, there is no difference.
The Dodsons, Stelling, Tulliver — they are all operating in a world where appearance and substance have become formally equivalent.
And Maggie, of course, is the one character who cannot manage that equivalence — which is why the novel breaks her.
That's a thread we'll follow much further as the episode continues — the question of what happens when a character of real substance is trapped in a world that only rewards performed respectability.
Oliver, James, Caroline — thank you.
Coming up: we look more closely at the economics of the Tulliver household and what ruin actually meant — socially, legally, and personally — for a family like this.
Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
We've been tracing the bond between Tom and Maggie Tulliver — and today we turn to the moments where that bond fractures.
From childhood anguish to the devastating final rejection, this is George Eliot at her most searching and her most painful.
Oliver Trevelyan is with us — actor, writer, and the man whose voice has given life to more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive.
Oliver brings his performer's ear to the rhythms of Eliot's prose — and no one is better at catching what she wrote for the voice.
Professor James Blackstone joins us — legal and social historian, a man who can tell you exactly what it meant, in material and legal terms, to be the Tullivers.
James has a particular eye for the institutions that shape these lives — and a dry fury about the injustices they encode.
And Caroline Woodcourt is here — book critic, lifelong reader of this novel, and the person in this room who feels most strongly about what Maggie Tulliver deserves.
Caroline has re-read this novel many times, and each time she finds something new to love — and something new to grieve.
Let's begin where the rift has its roots — in childhood, in those early asymmetries between Tom and Maggie.
What strikes me first, every single time, is that Eliot refuses to be superior about childhood suffering.
There's this extraordinary moment after Maggie has cut her hair — she's sitting among her black locks, weeping — and the narrator pivots outward.
The pivot is almost aggressive in how directly it addresses the reader.
Listen to how it lands:
That comparative — 'perhaps it was even more bitter' — that's the novelist doing something audacious.
She's not just defending Maggie's pain — she's suggesting it may exceed what adults suffer.
And the Ajax comparison just before it — 'helpless and despairing among her black locks as Ajax among the slaughtered sheep' — that's pure comic genius masking genuine tenderness.
The Ajax comparison always catches me off guard, even now.
It's absurd and it's completely right.
Maggie at eight years old, heroic in her catastrophe.
But what moves me even more is what Eliot does with Tom in that same passage.
She says Tom had 'a wonderful instinctive discernment of what would turn to his advantage or disadvantage.'
That word 'instinctive' is doing so much work.
It's not that Tom is calculating in a cold, premeditated way — it's that self-interest runs through him like a natural reflex.
And Eliot gives us that quietly, without condemnation — but the contrast with Maggie's helplessness is devastating.
I want to add one thing to that — because what Eliot is describing in Tom is not just a personality type.
It's the psychology that the social order was designed to produce in boys of his class.
Instrumental reasoning, pride in one's position, no appetite for self-examination.
Eliot puts it quite beautifully — Tom, when he 'broke the lash of his father's gigwhip by lashing the gate,' simply decided the whip shouldn't have got caught in the hinge.
He externalises fault. Every time, without fail.
That habit of mind — applied to a sister's reputation, a family's honour — has catastrophic consequences later in the novel.
And yet Eliot doesn't let us simply dismiss Tom, even in his worst moments.
There's a passage at Stelling's school that I find almost unbearably touching — because we see Tom's pride completely humiliated.
He's failing at Latin, failing at Euclid, he can't manage any of it — and so he turns, in desperation, to prayer.
But the prayers he knows are all learned by heart, and he's — and this is so Tom — reluctant to introduce an extempore passage for which he was 'not aware of any precedent.'
Even in prayer he needs the rules to be clear.
But then he does it — he whispers:
And then he considers how to pray about Euclid — which, I have to say, is one of the funniest sentences in the English novel.
That passage makes me laugh and then immediately feel guilty for laughing.
Because Eliot tells us that Tom had begun praying for Maggie when she was a baby.
That detail, tucked in parentheses — 'he had begun to pray for Maggie when she was a baby' — it undoes you.
The love is real. It has always been real.
Which is precisely what makes what Tom does to Maggie later so impossible to forgive — and so impossible to reduce to simple cruelty.
And between those poles — the praying boy and the man who casts his sister out — there's the ruin of the family.
Which Eliot renders in a single, devastating physical image.
Maggie sobbing, Tom holding her — and yet entirely elsewhere.
A black curtain of cloud fallen on his path.
That image tells you everything about how Tom will move through the rest of the novel — forward, only forward, nothing processed, nothing grieved.
And yet — there's that moment with the aunts, which is Tom at his most unexpectedly admirable.
He looks straight at Mrs Glegg — which takes nerve, I assure you — and says:
It's direct, it's practical, it's Tom — and it comes from genuine love for his mother.
The same rigidity that will destroy Maggie here shields his mother from humiliation.
That's the terrible coherence of Tom Tulliver.
Which brings us, inevitably, to the passage I find the most difficult in the novel.
Tom's rejection of Maggie — after she returns from her time on the river with Stephen Guest.
Eliot gives him the floor, and he uses it without mercy.
'You don't belong to me.' Four words.
From a legal and social standpoint, Tom is doing what the culture expects of him — protecting the family name, enforcing female respectability.
He is the mechanism of a system, and he doesn't know it.
And that is the novel's most devastating indictment — not of Tom, but of what Tom has been made into.
I don't fully accept that absolution.
Or rather — I accept the analysis, but I can't quite let Tom off the hook alongside it.
Because Eliot gives him 'tremulous rage' — he is trembling.
There's something in him that knows what he's doing and chooses to do it anyway.
'You have been a curse to your best friends.'
Best friends — he means himself. He means himself.
There is wounded love underneath every word of that speech — and that's what makes it so cruel, and so true to life.
Wounded love. That's exactly the phrase.
And it is, I think, what keeps this from being a simple novel about a cruel brother and a suffering sister.
Eliot insists on the full humanity of both — and charges us with holding both at once.
Coming up: we'll turn to what Maggie herself makes of all this — how she endures, and what endurance costs her.

segments.title: Comedy and Cruelty: The Dodson Way

utterances.text: Welcome back to The Mill on the Floss Unpacked.
Today we're in territory that Eliot does better than almost anyone: comedy that has a sharp edge — characters who are ridiculous and real at the same time.
And alongside that, the novel's darker current — what it costs to be good.
Oliver Trevelyan has spent more hours inside this novel's comic world than perhaps anyone — as a reader, a performer, a delighted audience of one.
James Blackstone is watching what those comic surfaces are concealing — the social machinery underneath.
And Caroline Woodcourt is here for the sentences themselves — the ones you have to read twice because they're so good.
Oliver — let's start with you and the mill itself.
The mill passage is one I come back to every time, because it does something so quietly unusual.
It gives Maggie an inner world of genuine intellectual richness — and locates it, brilliantly, inside an industrial building full of noise and flour dust.
Eliot writes that the mill was, and I want to read this carefully —
That phrase — a little world apart — is doing enormous work.
It's the first real sanctuary we see her inhabit, and Eliot earns it through sensation before she earns it through idea.
The din, the meal pouring, the scent — you feel it before you understand it.
But then — and this is where I start laughing out loud every time — we get the spiders.
Maggie has constructed an entire sociology of spider family relations based on the problem of dietary incompatibility.
A fat and floury spider — imagine performing that line — accustomed to take his fly well dusted with meal, must suffer a little at a cousin's table.
Eliot is showing us that this child's mind is already doing what novelists do — extending empathy to creatures most people never think about, and then building comic architecture on top of it.
The lady spiders mutually shocked at each other's appearance — that is a joke with a genuine sociological sting.
What I love is that the comedy is entirely sympathetic to Maggie, never at her expense.
The narrator is in on the joke with her, not above it.
And notice the detail about her hair — she comes out with her black hair powdered to a soft whiteness that made her dark eyes flash out with new fire.
That image does so much: it's comic and slightly wild and extraordinarily beautiful all at once.
Maggie in the mill is Maggie at her best — curious, alive, uncontained.
The mill is also, of course, the economic engine that defines the whole family's standing.
When Maggie treats it as a private playground and a theatre of imagination, there's a gentle irony the novel is already setting up.
This paradise of flour and sensation will eventually be lost — taken away by courts and creditors.
The child's sanctuary and the commodity that ruins the father are the same object.
Eliot is never sentimental about that double vision.
That double vision is exactly what makes Tom's fancy-dress scene so rich — because the comedy there comes from innocence about to encounter consequence.
Tom has gone to extraordinary lengths to look fearsome, and the narrator records every detail with completely straight-faced affection.
We're told —
The specificity of that — the horseshoe frown, the looking-glass, the sheer effort — is what makes it devastating.
Tom is trying so hard to be something he simply isn't, and Eliot finds that both funny and tender.
And Philip is there, watching — which gives the whole thing another layer.
Philip, who is physically constrained and knows it, is watching Tom perform a kind of bodily freedom that is pure theatre.
It was Philip who told Tom about the horseshoe frown in the first place, which Eliot slips in almost as an aside.
Philip gave Tom the idea for his own theatrical self-construction.
That tiny connection between them — in a friendship that will later become so fraught — is quietly heartbreaking.
What strikes me about that scene is how precisely Eliot documents the materials of performance.
Burnt cork, a red handkerchief, a comforter repurposed as a scarf — these are household objects of a specific social station.
Tom can't buy a costume; he improvises with what's available.
Even childhood play in this novel is constrained by what the family can afford.
Now — Bob Jakin and Mrs Glegg.
This is the scene I read aloud whenever someone tells me Victorian novels are dull.
Bob is a salesman of genius, and his pitch to Mrs Glegg is a masterclass in calibrated flattery.
He leads with the dog — the dog knows quality, the dog is drawn to good-looking ladies, the dog is a connoisseur.
And then, having softened her completely, he delivers the actual commercial argument, which goes —
Bottles with ornamental stoppers — I have never heard shop assistants described better in my life.
What makes that passage sing is the rhythm of it — it keeps accelerating.
One complaint piles on the next: the chins propped up, the stiff stock, the dinners extracted from calico.
And then the final insult — they're throttled till the lies are squeezed out of them, whether they will or no.
It's a speech that would bring down the house in a theatre.
But it's also a genuine portrait of a working man who has had to develop his entire personality as a survival tool.
Bob's attack on the shops is not merely comic — it's economically accurate.
Fixed-premises retail in the eighteen-fifties was genuinely more expensive than the itinerant packman trade, for exactly the reasons he gives: rent, staff wages, overheads.
Bob is also, crucially, reading Mrs Glegg's class identity correctly.
She is the kind of woman who prides herself on not being taken in — and he flatters precisely that self-image.
You can see through them shopmen, he says — and she can, and she knows she can, and now she will buy his calico.
The real cruelty in this novel, though, isn't in the comic scenes.
It's what Eliot does to Maggie in the later chapters — the internal battle she depicts with such forensic precision.
James has the passage — I'll hand over, because this is territory that deserves its due weight.
The passage from chapter fifty-two is one of the most morally searching pieces of prose in the English novel.
Eliot doesn't let Maggie be a simple heroine — she gives her the worst thoughts, the selfish thoughts, and she records them without flinching.
Why should not Lucy, why should not Philip, suffer?
That question, in Maggie's mind, is presented not as a moral failure but as a human truth.
She has suffered; she has renounced; no one has renounced anything for her.
And then Eliot delivers the answer, which is also the sentence I would put on the cover of any edition of this book —
Maiming the organs of her soul — that is not consolation; it is diagnosis.
I have to say, every time I read that sentence I have to stop.
Because it reframes the entire moral question of the novel.
It's not that Maggie must be good because goodness is rewarded or because God demands it.
It's that the self she would destroy in order to have what she wants is precisely the self that could enjoy having it.
Eliot is doing something deeply secular and deeply serious there.
And yet it's still Maggie — still the girl who slid down the grain heaps and worried about the floury spiders.
What the passage also shows is how completely Maggie has been abandoned by any social structure that might have helped her.
There is no institution — no education, no profession, no independent income — that gives her a path other than this.
Her moral battle is conducted in a vacuum of social support.
That is a structural cruelty — the cruelty of a society that starves people of choices and then judges them for the hunger.
And that is the tension at the heart of this novel — the comedy and the cruelty are not opposites.
The same sensibility that gave Maggie her floury spiders also gave her this impossible moral situation.
Oliver, James, Caroline — thank you.
We'll be back after the break with the novel's central battles over property, inheritance, and what it means to lose everything.

segments.title: Drowning in Duty: The Mill's Last Pages

utterances.text: We've arrived at the closing chapter of today's conversation — and, in many ways, at the emotional heart of the novel itself.
The Mill on the Floss is a book obsessed with duty — what we owe each other, what we owe ourselves, and what happens when those obligations collide.
To help us bring that home, I want to start with a small, quiet moment — Mr Tulliver on horseback, riding away from a dilapidated farm, and then turning back.
That scene is one of the great small moments in the novel, and it's all in the physical comedy of it — almost.
He rides out. He's resolved. He's a man of action.
And then Eliot says — and I love this — he appeared to be smitten by some sudden thought.
He turned his head from side to side in a melancholy way, as if he were looking at some painful object on more sides than one.
That parenthetical — on more sides than one — that's Eliot catching the exact shape of a man's grief.
And what breaks him? What turns the horse?
He says it aloud — to no one, to himself, to the lane:
"Poor little wench! she'll have nobody but Tom, belike, when I'm gone."
Five words of dialect and a man's whole heart is in them.
What kills me about that line is the word belike.
It means probably, roughly — it's a hedge, an uncertainty.
He doesn't know if Tom will be there for Maggie. He fears he won't.
And the reader, who knows Tom, feels the full weight of that belike.
That's Eliot doing something very subtle — she's giving Mr Tulliver a moment of prophetic sorrow without letting him know that's what it is.
That anxiety about Maggie's dependence is not merely tender — it's structurally accurate.
A woman in Maggie's position, without property, without a husband, without Tom's goodwill — she has essentially no standing.
Mr Tulliver knows this in his bones, even if he can't articulate it in those terms.
Which brings me to Wakem — because Tulliver's fate is threaded through with a kind of institutional cruelty that Eliot refuses to let us look away from.
She draws the parallel herself, quite directly:
"Mr Tulliver had a destiny as well as Œdipus, and in this case he might plead, like Œdipus, that his deed was inflicted on him rather than committed by him."
That's a startling comparison to make — and Eliot makes it without a trace of irony.
Tulliver is not Oedipus in scale, but the structural trap is the same: the world conspires, and the man walks into it.
And yet — and this is what I love about Tulliver — he's not a tragic hero in any conventional sense.
He's a muddled, proud, infuriating man who makes everything worse with his best intentions.
The Oedipus comparison only works because Eliot is entirely serious about the dignity of ordinary life.
The miller is as deserving of tragedy as the king. That's her whole argument.
And that argument about dignity — about the claims of ordinary life — runs straight into the novel's most beautiful passages about home and memory.
Caroline, you've spoken before about the passage where Eliot reflects on the meaning of childhood places. What does it do for you?
It undoes me, every time. Every single time.
Because Eliot is making a philosophical claim, but she wraps it in the most physical, sensory language.
Listen to what she says about those early scenes:

"There is no sense of ease like the ease we felt in those scenes where we were born, where objects became dear to us before we had known the labour of choice, and where the outer world seemed only an extension of our own personality."
The labour of choice. That phrase stops me cold.
Home is where you don't have to choose. The world just is what it is, and you belong to it.
And what Eliot makes us feel — agonizingly — is that Maggie can never fully rest in that ease. Not really.
There's also a quietly subversive joke in that passage — and Eliot buries it with a perfectly straight face.
She says — and I'm paraphrasing only slightly — that striving after improvement is what distinguishes man from the brute.
And then she completes the thought:
"or, to satisfy a scrupulous accuracy of definition, that distinguishes the British man from the foreign brute."
The Victorian ideology of progress — skewered in a single subordinate clause.
And yet she means everything else in that passage with complete sincerity. The elderberry bush is real. The memory is real.
That's what I mean when I say she's a writer who operates on multiple registers simultaneously.
The comedy and the tenderness are not in opposition — they're in the same sentence, breathing together.
And that elderberry bush — I adore that image. It's utterly unjustifiable as a preference, she admits it freely.
But it is, she says, the long companion of my existence, that wove itself into my joys when joys were vivid.
When joys were vivid. You can't improve on that.
And yet the novel insists that home, and ease, and belonging — all of it can be taken from you.
Which brings us to Maggie, and to Dr Kenn, and to what I think is one of the most quietly devastating passages in the book.
Dr Kenn is the one character in the novel who truly sees Maggie — who comprehends what she's done and why.
And Eliot shows us his anguish with extraordinary care.
He can see that marrying Stephen might be the least evil available. He understands the practical case.
But then Eliot gives us the counter-weight — the reason he cannot say it:
"her conscience must not be tampered with; the principle on which she had acted was a safer guide than any balancing of consequences."
He respects her moral integrity too much to override it, even to save her.
That is a devastating kind of love — to hold someone's conscience sacred even when it destroys them.
What Eliot is also doing there is making a serious argument about the limits of consequentialist ethics.
Dr Kenn's position is essentially Kantian — you don't tamper with the moral agent, even if tampering would produce a better outcome.
And that position leaves him — and Maggie — with no good path.
Each immediate step was clogged with evil — that's Eliot's phrase, and it's perfectly chosen.
Not one great catastrophe, but a slow, grinding obstruction at every turn.
And it ends in flood water. It ends in those two, together, and then gone.
I have never made my peace with that ending. I don't think you're supposed to.
What Eliot gives you is not resolution — it's recognition.
The recognition that some lives are shaped by forces too deep to outrun — by duty, by memory, by love — and that those forces can be simultaneously beautiful and fatal.
Simultaneously beautiful and fatal — I think that's as fine a summary of The Mill on the Floss as I've heard.
Oliver Trevelyan, James Blackstone, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you, all three, for a conversation that has done full justice to an extraordinary novel.
The Mill on the Floss reminds us, again and again, that ordinary lives contain all the grandeur and all the grief that literature can hold.
We hope you'll return to the novel — and to us — with new eyes.

c3:p79.text:
Plotting covetousness and deliberate contrivance, in order to compass a selfish
end, are nowhere abundant but in the world of the dramatist: they demand too
intense a mental action for many of our fellow-parishioners to be guilty of
them. It is easy enough to spoil the lives of our neighbours without taking so
much trouble; we can do it by lazy acquiescence and lazy omission, by trivial
falsities for which we hardly know a reason, by small frauds neutralised by
small extravagances, by maladroit flatteries, and clumsily improvised
insinuations. We live from hand to mouth, most of us, with a small family of
immediate desires; we do little else than snatch a morsel to satisfy the hungry
brood, rarely thinking of seed-corn or the next year’s crop.
c3:p79.summary: The narrator offers profound reflection that most moral failures result not from deliberate villainy but from small, thoughtless acts, lazy compliance, and accumulated minor dishonestries.
c3:p79.best_quote: It is easy enough to spoil the lives of our neighbours without taking so much trouble; we can do it by lazy acquiescence and lazy omission, by trivial falsities for which we hardly know a reason, by small frauds neutralised by small extravagances, by maladroit flatteries, and clumsily improvised insinuations

c14:p100.text:
But when this small apparatus of shallow quickness was fetched away in the gig
by Luke, and the study was once more quite lonely for Tom, he missed her
grievously. He had really been brighter, and had got through his lessons
better, since she had been there; and she had asked Mr Stelling so many
questions about the Roman Empire, and whether there really ever was a man who
said, in Latin, “I would not buy it for a farthing or a rotten
nut,” or whether that had only been turned into Latin, that Tom had
actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been
people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning
it through the medium of the Eton Grammar. This luminous idea was a great
addition to his historical acquirements during this half-year, which were
otherwise confined to an epitomised history of the Jews.
c14:p100.summary: Tom grieves Maggie's departure and credits her insightful questions about the Roman Empire with expanding his historical understanding beyond his textbooks.
c14:p100.best_quote: he had actually come to a dim understanding of the fact that there had once been people upon the earth who were so fortunate as to know Latin without learning it through the medium of the Eton Grammar

c28:p29.text: “Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o’er.”
c28:p29.summary: Mr Tulliver tells Maggie that even though she loves him, he will never have another chance at life or redemption.
c28:p29.best_quote: Ay, my little wench, but I shall never live twice o'er

c53:p29.text:
“That seems right—at first; but when I look further, I’m sure
it is  not  right. Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides
doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves. They mean renouncing
whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us,—whatever would
cause misery to those whom the course of our lives has made dependent on us. If
we—if I had been better, nobler, those claims would have been so strongly
present with me,—I should have felt them pressing on my heart so
continually, just as they do now in the moments when my conscience is
awake,—that the opposite feeling would never have grown in me, as it has
done; it would have been quenched at once, I should have prayed for help so
earnestly, I should have rushed away as we rush from hideous danger. I feel no
excuse for myself, none. I should never have failed toward Lucy and Philip as I
have done, if I had not been weak, selfish, and hard,—able to think of
their pain without a pain to myself that would have destroyed all temptation.
Oh, what is Lucy feeling now? She believed in me—she loved me—she
was so good to me. Think of her——”
c53:p29.summary: Maggie passionately explains that faithfulness means renouncing self-interest to honor the trust others have placed in us; she expresses anguish over her betrayal of Lucy and Philip, and argues she should have prayed harder to resist temptation.
c53:p29.best_quote: Faithfulness and constancy mean something else besides doing what is easiest and pleasantest to ourselves. They mean renouncing whatever is opposed to the reliance others have in us.

c13:p5.text:
Mrs Glegg being in this state of satisfaction in her own lofty magnanimity, I
leave you to judge what effect was produced on her by the reception of a short
letter from Mr Tulliver that very evening, after Mrs Pullet’s
departure, informing her that she needn’t trouble her mind about her five
hundred pounds, for it should be paid back to her in the course of the next
month at farthest, together with the interest due thereon until the time of
payment. And furthermore, that Mr Tulliver had no wish to behave uncivilly to
Mrs Glegg, and she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he
desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.
c13:p5.summary: Mr Tulliver writes to Mrs Glegg announcing he will repay her five hundred pounds within a month and neither desires nor requires her favours, completely inverting her anticipated reconciliation.
c13:p5.best_quote: she was welcome to his house whenever she liked to come, but he desired no favours from her, either for himself or his children.

c15:p18.text:
Mrs Tulliver, as we have seen, was not without influence over her husband. No
woman is; she can always incline him to do either what she wishes, or the
reverse; and on the composite impulses that were threatening to hurry Mr
Tulliver into “law,” Mrs Tulliver’s monotonous pleading had
doubtless its share of force; it might even be comparable to that proverbial
feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel’s back;
though, on a strictly impartial view, the blame ought rather to lie with the
previous weight of feathers which had already placed the back in such imminent
peril that an otherwise innocent feather could not settle on it without
mischief. Not that Mrs Tulliver’s feeble beseeching could have had this
feather’s weight in virtue of her single personality; but whenever she
departed from entire assent to her husband, he saw in her the representative of
the Dodson family; and it was a guiding principle with Mr Tulliver to let the
Dodsons know that they were not to domineer over  him , or—more
specifically—that a male Tulliver was far more than equal to four female
Dodsons, even though one of them was Mrs Glegg.
c15:p18.summary: The narrator observes that Mrs Tulliver's weak pleading against law has cumulative force when combined with his fear of Dodson influence, though she is not powerful in herself.
c15:p18.best_quote: it might even be comparable to that proverbial feather which has the credit or discredit of breaking the camel's back

c15:p19.text:
But not even a direct argument from that typical Dodson female herself against
his going to law could have heightened his disposition toward it so much as the
mere thought of Wakem, continually freshened by the sight of the too able
attorney on market-days. Wakem, to his certain knowledge, was (metaphorically
speaking) at the bottom of Pivart’s irrigation; Wakem had tried to make
Dix stand out, and go to law about the dam; it was unquestionably Wakem who had
caused Mr Tulliver to lose the suit about the right of road and the bridge
that made a thoroughfare of his land for every vagabond who preferred an
opportunity of damaging private property to walking like an honest man along
the highroad; all lawyers were more or less rascals, but Wakem’s
rascality was of that peculiarly aggravated kind which placed itself in
opposition to that form of right embodied in Mr Tulliver’s interests and
opinions. And as an extra touch of bitterness, the injured miller had recently,
in borrowing the five hundred pounds, been obliged to carry a little business
to Wakem’s office on his own account. A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool
as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game! And it was vexatious
that Lawyer Gore was not more like him, but was a bald, round-featured man,
with bland manners and fat hands; a game-cock that you would be rash to bet
upon against Wakem. Gore was a sly fellow. His weakness did not lie on the side
of scrupulosity; but the largest amount of winking, however significant, is not
equivalent to seeing through a stone wall; and confident as Mr Tulliver was in
his principle that water was water, and in the direct inference that Pivart had
not a leg to stand on in this affair of irrigation, he had an uncomfortable
suspicion that Wakem had more law to show against this (rationally)
irrefragable inference than Gore could show for it. But then, if they went to
law, there was a chance for Mr Tulliver to employ Counsellor Wylde on his
side, instead of having that admirable bully against him; and the prospect of
seeing a witness of Wakem’s made to perspire and become confounded, as
Mr Tulliver’s witness had once been, was alluring to the love of
retributive justice.
c15:p19.summary: The narrator details Mr Tulliver's bitter conviction that Wakem orchestrates all his legal troubles and has humiliated him repeatedly; reveals his visceral hatred of the lawyer.
c15:p19.best_quote: A hook-nosed glib fellow! as cool as a cucumber,—always looking so sure of his game!

c25:p73.text:
Their mother came in now, and Maggie rushed away, that her burst of tears,
which she felt must come, might not happen till she was safe upstairs. They
were very bitter tears; everybody in the world seemed so hard and unkind to
Maggie; there was no indulgence, no fondness, such as she imagined when she
fashioned the world afresh in her own thoughts. In books there were people who
were always agreeable or tender, and delighted to do things that made one
happy, and who did not show their kindness by finding fault. The world outside
the books was not a happy one, Maggie felt; it seemed to be a world where
people behaved the best to those they did not pretend to love, and that did not
belong to them. And if life had no love in it, what else was there for Maggie?
Nothing but poverty and the companionship of her mother’s narrow griefs,
perhaps of her father’s heart-cutting childish dependence. There is no
hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants,
and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others; though we
who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the
future lightened the blind sufferer’s present.
c25:p73.summary: Maggie rushes upstairs with bitter tears, feeling the world is hard and unkind; the narrator reveals her anguish: she expected love and tenderness from others as she imagines from books, but finds a harsh world where affection shows itself as fault-finding, and she sees no hope without love.
c25:p73.best_quote: There is no hopelessness so sad as that of early youth, when the soul is made up of wants, and has no long memories, no superadded life in the life of others; though we who looked on think lightly of such premature despair, as if our vision of the future lightened the blind sufferer's present.

c37:p53.text:
“Do what  I  require,” said Tom. “I can’t trust
you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you. Put your hand on this Bible, and
say, ‘I renounce all private speech and intercourse with Philip Wakem
from this time forth.’ Else you will bring shame on us all, and grief on
my father; and what is the use of my exerting myself and giving up everything
else for the sake of paying my father’s debts, if you are to bring
madness and vexation on him, just when he might be easy and hold up his head
once more?”
c37:p53.summary: Tom insists Maggie must put her hand on the Bible and speak the exact words of renunciation, claiming he cannot trust her, that she lacks consistency, and that while he has been working to pay their father's debts and restore family respectability, she has done everything to destroy both.
c37:p53.best_quote: I can't trust you, Maggie. There is no consistency in you... while I have been contriving and working that my father may have some peace of mind before he dies,—working for the respectability of our family,—you have done all you can to destroy both

c10:p1.text:
Maggie said nothing, but turned away from her with a deeper frown. As long as
Tom seemed to prefer Lucy to her, Lucy made part of his unkindness. Maggie
would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty
little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but
then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been
left to Maggie to pet and make much of her. As it was, she was actually
beginning to think that she should like to make Lucy cry by slapping or
pinching her, especially as it might vex Tom, whom it was of no use to slap,
even if she dared, because he didn’t mind it. And if Lucy hadn’t
been there, Maggie was sure he would have got friends with her sooner.
c10:p1.summary: Maggie's jealousy transforms her affection into potential cruelty; she blames Lucy for Tom's unkindness and fantasizes about hurting her to vex Tom.
c10:p1.best_quote: Maggie would have thought a little while ago that she could never be cross with pretty little Lucy, any more than she could be cruel to a little white mouse; but then, Tom had always been quite indifferent to Lucy before, and it had been left to Maggie to pet and make much of her.

c11:p0.text:
Maggie’s intentions, as usual, were on a larger scale than Tom imagined.
The resolution that gathered in her mind, after Tom and Lucy had walked away,
was not so simple as that of going home. No! she would run away and go to the
gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more. That was by no means a new idea
to Maggie; she had been so often told she was like a gypsy, and “half
wild,” that when she was miserable it seemed to her the only way of
escaping opprobrium, and being entirely in harmony with circumstances, would be
to live in a little brown tent on the commons; the gypsies, she considered,
would gladly receive her and pay her much respect on account of her superior
knowledge. She had once mentioned her views on this point to Tom and suggested
that he should stain his face brown, and they should run away together; but Tom
rejected the scheme with contempt, observing that gypsies were thieves, and
hardly got anything to eat and had nothing to drive but a donkey. To-day
however, Maggie thought her misery had reached a pitch at which gypsydom was
her refuge, and she rose from her seat on the roots of the tree with the sense
that this was a great crisis in her life; she would run straight away till she
came to Dunlow Common, where there would certainly be gypsies; and cruel Tom,
and the rest of her relations who found fault with her, should never see her
any more. She thought of her father as she ran along, but she reconciled
herself to the idea of parting with him, by determining that she would secretly
send him a letter by a small gypsy, who would run away without telling where
she was, and just let him know that she was well and happy, and always loved
him very much.
c11:p0.summary: Maggie resolves to run away to the gypsies after Tom's rejection, a fantasy she has long harboured as a way to escape family reproach and find harmony with her perceived wild nature.
c11:p0.best_quote: No! she would run away and go to the gypsies, and Tom should never see her any more.

c11:p35.text:
Her ideas about the gypsies had undergone a rapid modification in the last five
minutes. From having considered them very respectful companions, amenable to
instruction, she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon
as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking; the suspicion crossed
her that the fierce-eyed old man was in fact the Devil, who might drop that
transparent disguise at any moment, and turn either into the grinning
blacksmith, or else a fiery-eyed monster with dragon’s wings. It was no
use trying to eat the stew, and yet the thing she most dreaded was to offend
the gypsies, by betraying her extremely unfavourable opinion of them; and she
wondered, with a keenness of interest that no theologian could have exceeded,
whether, if the Devil were really present, he would know her thoughts.
c11:p35.summary: Maggie's fantasy collapses into paranoid horror as she imagines the gypsies as cannibals and the fierce-eyed man as the Devil.
c11:p35.best_quote: she had begun to think that they meant perhaps to kill her as soon as it was dark, and cut up her body for gradual cooking.

c51:p29.text:
But to minds strongly marked by the positive and negative qualities that create
severity,—strength of will, conscious rectitude of purpose, narrowness of
imagination and intellect, great power of self-control, and a disposition to
exert control over others,—prejudices come as the natural food of
tendencies which can get no sustenance out of that complex, fragmentary,
doubt-provoking knowledge which we call truth. Let a prejudice be bequeathed,
carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the
eye,—however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is
something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of
spontaneous ideas, something to impose on others with the authority of
conscious right; it is at once a staff and a baton. Every prejudice that will
answer these purposes is self-evident. Our good, upright Tom Tulliver’s
mind was of this class; his inward criticism of his father’s faults did
not prevent him from adopting his father’s prejudice; it was a prejudice
against a man of lax principle and lax life, and it was a meeting-point for all
the disappointed feelings of family and personal pride. Other feelings added
their force to produce Tom’s bitter repugnance to Philip, and to
Maggie’s union with him; and notwithstanding Lucy’s power over her
strong-willed cousin, she got nothing but a cold refusal ever to sanction such
a marriage; “but of course Maggie could do as she liked,—she had
declared her determination to be independent. For Tom’s part, he held
himself bound by his duty to his father’s memory, and by every manly
feeling, never to consent to any relation with the Wakems.”
c51:p29.summary: The narrator characterizes Tom's mind as rigid and wedded to inherited prejudice; his narrow imagination and strong will make him incapable of questioning paternal grievances or considering Maggie's happiness with Philip.
c51:p29.best_quote: Let a prejudice be bequeathed, carried in the air, adopted by hearsay, caught in through the eye,—however it may come, these minds will give it a habitation; it is something to assert strongly and bravely, something to fill up the void of spontaneous ideas, something to impose on others with the authority of conscious right

c28:p64.text:
“Say no more, Tom, say no more; I’ve had enough for this day. Give
me a kiss, Bessy, and let us bear one another no ill-will; we shall never be
young again—this world’s been too many for me.”
c28:p64.summary: Mr Tulliver asks Tom to cease arguing, seeks reconciliation with his wife, and acknowledges that he and they are broken by forces beyond their control.
c28:p64.best_quote: we shall never be young again—this world's been too many for me

c6:p8.text:
“Well, well, do as you like, Bessy,” said Mr Tulliver, taking up
his hat and walking out to the mill. Few wives were more submissive than Mrs
Tulliver on all points unconnected with her family relations; but she had been
a Miss Dodson, and the Dodsons were a very respectable family indeed,—as
much looked up to as any in their own parish, or the next to it. The Miss
Dodsons had always been thought to hold up their heads very high, and no one
was surprised the two eldest had married so well,—not at an early age,
for that was not the practice of the Dodson family. There were particular ways
of doing everything in that family: particular ways of bleaching the linen, of
making the cowslip wine, curing the hams, and keeping the bottled gooseberries;
so that no daughter of that house could be indifferent to the privilege of
having been born a Dodson, rather than a Gibson or a Watson. Funerals were
always conducted with peculiar propriety in the Dodson family: the hat-bands
were never of a blue shade, the gloves never split at the thumb, everybody was
a mourner who ought to be, and there were always scarfs for the bearers. When
one of the family was in trouble or sickness, all the rest went to visit the
unfortunate member, usually at the same time, and did not shrink from uttering
the most disagreeable truths that correct family feeling dictated; if the
illness or trouble was the sufferer’s own fault, it was not in the
practice of the Dodson family to shrink from saying so. In short, there was in
this family a peculiar tradition as to what was the right thing in household
management and social demeanour, and the only bitter circumstance attending
this superiority was a painful inability to approve the condiments or the
conduct of families ungoverned by the Dodson tradition. A female Dodson, when
in “strange houses,” always ate dry bread with her tea, and
declined any sort of preserves, having no confidence in the butter, and
thinking that the preserves had probably begun to ferment from want of due
sugar and boiling. There were some Dodsons less like the family than others,
that was admitted; but in so far as they were “kin,” they were of
necessity better than those who were “no kin.” And it is remarkable
that while no individual Dodson was satisfied with any other individual Dodson,
each was satisfied, not only with him or herself, but with the Dodsons
collectively. The feeblest member of a family—the one who has the least
character—is often the merest epitome of the family habits and
traditions; and Mrs Tulliver was a thorough Dodson, though a mild one, as
small-beer, so long as it is anything, is only describable as very weak ale:
and though she had groaned a little in her youth under the yoke of her elder
sisters, and still shed occasional tears at their sisterly reproaches, it was
not in Mrs Tulliver to be an innovator on the family ideas. She was thankful to
have been a Dodson, and to have one child who took after her own family, at
least in his features and complexion, in liking salt and in eating beans, which
a Tulliver never did.
c6:p8.summary: Extended digression on Dodson family tradition, their elaborate codes of propriety, household management, and social superiority, establishing Mrs Tulliver as quintessentially Dodson despite her mildness.
c6:p8.best_quote: a female Dodson, when in 'strange houses,' always ate dry bread with her tea, and declined any sort of preserves, having no confidence in the butter

c8:p5.text:
Mr Tulliver, when under the influence of a strong feeling, had a promptitude
in action that may seem inconsistent with that painful sense of the
complicated, puzzling nature of human affairs under which his more
dispassionate deliberations were conducted; but it is really not improbable
that there was a direct relation between these apparently contradictory
phenomena, since I have observed that for getting a strong impression that a
skein is tangled there is nothing like snatching hastily at a single thread. It
was owing to this promptitude that Mr Tulliver was on horseback soon after
dinner the next day (he was not dyspeptic) on his way to Basset to see his
sister Moss and her husband. For having made up his mind irrevocably that he
would pay Mrs Glegg her loan of five hundred pounds, it naturally occurred to
him that he had a promissory note for three hundred pounds lent to his
brother-in-law Moss; and if the said brother-in-law could manage to pay in the
money within a given time, it would go far to lessen the fallacious air of
inconvenience which Mr Tulliver’s spirited step might have worn in the
eyes of weak people who require to know precisely  how  a thing is to be
done before they are strongly confident that it will be easy.
c8:p5.summary: The narrator explains Mr Tulliver's characteristic pattern: his impulsive decisiveness when emotionally aroused, contrasting with his usual recognition of life's complexity; he decides to call in Moss's three-hundred-pound debt to offset his own obligation to Mrs Glegg.
c8:p5.best_quote: it is really not improbable that there was a direct relation between these apparently contradictory phenomena, since I have observed that for getting a strong impression that a skein is tangled there is nothing like snatching hastily at a single thread.

c11:p34.text:
Maggie Tulliver, you perceive, was by no means that well trained, well-informed
young person that a small female of eight or nine necessarily is in these days;
she had only been to school a year at St Ogg’s, and had so few books
that she sometimes read the dictionary; so that in travelling over her small
mind you would have found the most unexpected ignorance as well as unexpected
knowledge. She could have informed you that there was such a word as
“polygamy,” and being also acquainted with
“polysyllable,” she had deduced the conclusion that
“poly” mean “many”; but she had had no idea that
gypsies were not well supplied with groceries, and her thoughts generally were
